description: A middle-grades Civil War course built from the free lesson plans that National Park Service rangers and historians wrote for the places where it happened, from Underground Railroad sites and Harpers Ferry to Manassas, Antietam, Gettysburg, Andersonville, and Appomattox. Each day your child works through one park lesson online: maps, letters, photographs, and primary documents, then a short writing or discussion activity. Every lesson plan and handout is free on nps.gov.
includes: 26 lessons in 5 units, from the road to war through emancipation
Link to the National Park Service lesson page for every lesson, plus key handouts
Primary sources: soldiers' letters, maps, photographs, pension files, and the Emancipation Proclamation
Map work, letter writing, debate, and one math lesson using real prison records

units.title: Unit 1: Slavery, Freedom Seekers, and a Nation Dividing

lessons.title: Seeking Sanctuary on the Underground Railroad
steps: Warm up: write two sentences on what freedom means to you
Watch the park's short 'Seeking Sanctuary' ranger video and retell its main ideas
Make a Venn diagram comparing the escape route south to Spanish Florida with the routes north to Canada
Look at the Network to Freedom map and find Fort Mose and Castillo de San Marcos

links.label: Lesson plan: Seeking Sanctuary (Castillo de San Marcos NM)

questions: Before there was a route north to Canada, which way did some freedom seekers in the British colonies escape?
What made Fort Mose special?
answers: South, to Spanish Florida (St. Augustine)
It was the first legally recognized free Black settlement in what became the United States

lessons.title: Harriet Tubman: Brave Woman or Just Plain Crazy?
steps: Look at a portrait of Harriet Tubman and list what you already know about her
Work through pages of the free Underground Railroad Junior Ranger booklet
Gather at least three pieces of evidence about why she escaped and why she went back
Write a short argument answering the lesson's question, and explain her impact

links.label: Lesson plan: Harriet Tubman (Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad NHP)
Underground Railroad Junior Ranger booklet (PDF)

questions: In what state was Harriet Tubman born into slavery?
Name two roles Tubman had besides Underground Railroad conductor.
What risks did she take each time she returned south?
answers: Maryland (Dorchester County, on the Eastern Shore)
Any two of: abolitionist, Civil War spy or scout, nurse, suffragist, humanitarian
Being caught and sent back into slavery, punished, or killed
lessons.notes: The lesson suggests a picture book and a TV trailer as hooks; a library biography works just as well.

lessons.title: Bleeding Kansas: One Decision, Many Problems
steps: Review the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act
Watch the Fort Scott 'Bleeding Kansas' video
Write a short, persuasive letter to a congressman from the point of view of someone living in 1854
Discuss: did your letter appeal to feelings or to reasons?

links.label: Lesson plan: Border Conflict (Fort Scott NHS)

questions: What is popular sovereignty?
Why did the Kansas-Nebraska Act upset many Northerners?
answers: Letting the people of a territory vote on whether to allow slavery
It opened land the Missouri Compromise had closed to slavery, so the compromise had to be repealed

lessons.title: Incident at Harpers Ferry: Slavery and John Brown
steps: Write a paragraph: is it ever okay to use violence to bring about needed change?
Research the lesson's 'History Detective' questions about slavery in North America
Read 'John Brown: Just the Facts' and circle the three most important facts
Decide where you stand: was Brown right to use violence? Explain your reasons aloud

links.label: Lesson plan: Incident at Harpers Ferry (Harpers Ferry NHP)

questions: Where did John Brown fight against slavery in 1855 to 1857?
What did the Dred Scott decision say about whether an enslaved man could sue in federal court?
answers: Kansas
It said he was not a citizen, so he could not sue
lessons.notes: The 'Rounds' reading uses real pre-war newspaper ads about enslaved people; preview it first.

lessons.title: A Nation Divided: Compromises and Their Limits
steps: Read the NPS articles on John C. Calhoun and James L. Petigru and compare them in a Venn diagram
Use the historical maps to fill in the 'Chart the Maps' sheet: free or slave, 1820 to 1854
Read the agreed statement of facts in the Dred Scott case and answer who, where, and why

links.label: Lesson plan: A Nation Divided (Kennesaw Mountain NBP)
Chart the Maps student sheet (PDF)

questions: Calhoun and Petigru were both South Carolinians. Which one was a Unionist?
Name three events from 1820 to 1857 that raised tension between North and South.
answers: James L. Petigru
Any three of: Missouri Compromise, Mexican War, Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska Act, Dred Scott decision
lessons.notes: Choose one or two of the three activities per sitting; this can stretch over two days.

lessons.title: Dear Diary: Abraham Lincoln's Reflections
steps: Write about a person or event that had a big effect on your life
Read Lincoln's 'House Divided' speech and his farewell to Springfield; note key words, people, and events
Write a journal entry as Lincoln might have, quoting one of the sources

links.label: Lesson plan: Dear Diary (Lincoln Boyhood NM)
House Divided speech (PDF)
Farewell address to Springfield (PDF)

questions: What did Lincoln mean when he said a house divided against itself cannot stand?
Did Lincoln keep a diary?
answers: The country could not last forever half slave and half free
No; we learn his thoughts from speeches, letters, and other sources

lessons.title: Fort Pickens and the Outbreak of the Civil War
steps: Look at the aerial photo of Fort Pickens and guess what it was for
Study the 1861 map of Pensacola's harbor forts
Read 'The Civil War in Pensacola Area' and the Chase and Slemmer meeting
Activity: decide whether you would have surrendered the fort, and defend your choice

links.label: Lesson: Fort Pickens and the Outbreak of the Civil War (Teaching with Historic Places)

questions: Why was Pensacola Bay a valuable prize?
What did Lieutenant Slemmer do on the day Florida seceded?
Which other fort, like Fort Pickens, needed supplies when Lincoln took office?
answers: Its safe harbor and navy yard (docks, supplies, shipbuilding)
He moved all his men into Fort Pickens
Fort Sumter

lessons.title: Joining Up! Why Young Men Enlisted
steps: Sort the 'reasons to enlist in 1861' cards from least to most important
Move ahead to 1862: after so many deaths, would the reasons change? Sort them again
Take on the identity of a real soldier of the 126th New York and introduce yourself
Read the U.S. oath of allegiance aloud

links.label: Lesson plan: The Battle of Harpers Ferry 1862, Joining Up! (Harpers Ferry NHP)
Reasons young men joined the armies in 1861 (PDF)

questions: What is the difference between a regiment and a company?
In mid-1862, how many more volunteers did Lincoln call for?
answers: A regiment is a larger unit led by a colonel and made up of several companies

lessons.title: First Battle of Manassas: An End to Innocence
steps: Find Manassas Junction on the lesson's 1861 maps and say why both armies wanted it
Read Major Sullivan Ballou's last letter and the letters of Private J. W. Reid
Read about Judith Henry, the widow whose home stood on the battlefield
Write a letter home as a soldier after the battle

links.label: Lesson page: First Battle of Manassas (Teaching with Historic Places)
Full lesson plan (PDF)

questions: What was the date of the first battle of Manassas?
What did Northerners usually call this battle?
How did the battle change the way Americans thought about the war?
answers: Bull Run
They stopped thinking of it as a short adventure and saw it would be long and costly

units.title: Unit 3: 1862, Rivers, Refuge, and the Bloodiest Day

lessons.title: Fortifications at Fort Donelson
steps: Find the Tennessee and Cumberland Rivers and Forts Henry, Heiman, and Donelson on the park map
Complete the park's fortifications worksheet
Sketch an earthen fort with its earthworks and abatis, or write two paragraphs about it

links.label: Lesson plan: Fortifications (Fort Donelson NB)
Fortifications worksheet (PDF)

questions: Why did the Confederates build these forts just south of Kentucky instead of farther north?
What is an abatis?
Which of the three forts is now under water?
answers: They could not violate Kentucky's neutrality
Felled trees with sharpened tops placed as a barrier in front of earthworks
Fort Henry

lessons.title: The Free State at Fort Donelson
steps: Read the background on enslaved laborers who built the forts and on the 1862 Union victory
Study the postwar sketch of the 'Free State' near the national cemetery
Read parts of Caroline Dorris's widow's pension file and list what it tells about her life

links.label: Lesson plan: The Free State at Fort Donelson (Fort Donelson NB)
Declaration for Widow's Pension (PDF)

questions: Why did freedom seekers come to Union-held forts?
About how many formerly enslaved people lived at Fort Donelson by the winter of 1863?
answers: For protection, food, shelter, and freedom
Nearly 300
lessons.notes: The handwritten pension papers are hard to read; read them together and take turns.

lessons.title: Chatham Plantation: Witness to the Civil War
steps: Find Chatham on its bluff above the Rappahannock River opposite Fredericksburg
Read how the war changed the Lacy family's home and how armies used it
Read about Chatham as a field hospital after the Battle of Fredericksburg
Write a letter home as a soldier, nurse, or member of the Lacy family

links.label: Lesson page: Chatham Plantation (Teaching with Historic Places)
Full lesson plan (PDF)

questions: Which president visited Chatham in 1862?
Name two famous volunteers who helped wounded soldiers at Chatham.
answers: Abraham Lincoln
Clara Barton and Walt Whitman

lessons.title: Antietam: The Bloodiest Day and Hope for Freedom
steps: Watch an animated map or read the park brochure about September 17, 1862
Look at the linked historic photographs and eyewitness accounts
Write and illustrate a front page of a newspaper reporting the battle and its meaning

links.label: Lesson plan: The Bloodiest Day in American History (Antietam NB)

questions: About how many soldiers were killed, wounded, or missing at Antietam?
What did President Lincoln issue after the battle?
answers: More than 23,000
The preliminary Emancipation Proclamation
lessons.notes: The lesson plans three class periods; at home, spread the newspaper over two or three days.

lessons.title: War at Your Doorstep: The Mumma Family at Antietam
steps: Look at the battlefield map and the Mumma farm site plan
Read 'A House was Burning' and the reading on slavery on the Mumma farm
Look at the family's claim for damages and list what they lost

links.label: Lesson page: War at Your Doorstep (Antietam NB)
Full lesson plan (PDF)

questions: Who burned the Mumma farm, and why?
What happened to Lucy Young in 1856?
answers: Confederate soldiers, so Union sharpshooters could not use the buildings
Samuel Mumma set her free (a deed of manumission)

lessons.title: Clara Barton: Angel of the Battlefield
steps: Read 'Clara Barton, Advocate for Human Rights'
Read about the American Red Cross and the women who went to the field
Activity: plan how a local group could help after a disaster

links.label: Lesson: Clara Barton's House (Teaching with Historic Places)

questions: What job did Clara Barton have in Washington before the war?
After the war, what did she spend four years doing?
What organization did she found?
answers: Patent clerk
Identifying missing soldiers
The American Red Cross

units.title: Unit 4: 1863 to 1864, Emancipation, Turning Points, and Hard War

lessons.title: War Has Been Declared: The Emancipation Proclamation
steps: Watch the short NPS video 'A New Birth of Freedom'
Read the Emancipation Proclamation one paragraph at a time and write a one-sentence summary of each
Read about the Atlanta Campaign and study its map

links.label: Lesson plan: War Has Been Declared (Kennesaw Mountain NBP)

questions: Which enslaved people did the Emancipation Proclamation declare free?
What is a proclamation?
answers: Those in areas still in rebellion against the United States
An important public or official announcement
lessons.notes: The Ambrose Bierce story in Activity 3 is grim; preview it before using.

lessons.title: Choices and Commitments: The Soldiers at Gettysburg
steps: Use Map 2 to follow the three days of fighting, July 1 to 3, 1863
Read 'Three Days of Carnage at Gettysburg' and answer its questions
Read the soldiers' accounts and compare their views
Read the Gettysburg Address aloud and copy one sentence

links.label: Lesson: Choices and Commitments, the Soldiers at Gettysburg (Teaching with Historic Places)

questions: What shape did the Union line form on July 2?
What was the name of Lee's final attack on July 3?
About how many casualties did Gettysburg cause?
answers: A fishhook
Pickett's Charge
About 51,000
lessons.notes: Two of the soldier accounts are excerpts from copyrighted books that the lesson reprints with permission; read them on the NPS page only.

lessons.title: The 1st Kansas Colored Infantry
steps: Watch the Fort Scott video on the 1st Kansas Colored Volunteer Infantry
Read the officers' quotations about the regiment
Put the regiment's battles from 1862 to 1864 on a timeline and a map

links.label: Lesson plan: 1st Kansas Colored Infantry (Fort Scott NHS)

questions: At which battle did the 1st Kansas Colored first fight, in October 1862?
Name one battle the regiment fought in Indian Territory.
answers: Island Mound, Missouri
Any of: Cabin Creek, Honey Springs, Flat Rock Creek, Timber Hills

lessons.title: Neither Cold Nor a Harbor: Archeology at Cold Harbor
steps: Read the background on the Overland Campaign and the June 1864 battle
Look at the 3D model of a canteen cut down into a shovel
Use the maps, readings, and images handouts to complete the student worksheet

links.label: Lesson plan: Neither Cold Nor a Harbor (Richmond NBP)
Student worksheet (Word)

questions: What was the Union army's main goal in the Overland Campaign?
Why did soldiers turn a canteen into a shovel?
answers: To capture Richmond, the Confederate capital
They had no shovels and needed to dig earthworks for protection

lessons.title: Civilian War Experience: Kennesaw Mountain
steps: Discuss what happens to a town when a battle is fought there
Read the account of Minerva McClatchey or Lucinda Hardage
Fill in the 'Questions, Problems, or Concerns' sheet: five problems and five actions

links.label: Lesson plan: Civilian War Experience (Kennesaw Mountain NBP)
Questions, Problems, or Concerns worksheet (PDF)

questions: Why read accounts by civilians, and not only by soldiers?
Which campaign was the Battle of Kennesaw Mountain part of?
answers: They show how a battle hurt families at home: their food, homes, and safety
The Atlanta Campaign

lessons.title: When War Hits Home: The Election of 1864
steps: Read the background on Peninsula, Ohio, a town on the Ohio and Erie Canal
Read excerpts from the letters of Lt. George Waterman and Sgt. Levi Boodey
Compare the 1864 Democratic and Republican platforms, then vote as Peninsula voters might have

links.label: Lesson plan: When War Hits Home (Cuyahoga Valley NP)
Boodey letters (Word)
Democratic Party platform, 1864 (Word)

questions: Which two men ran for president in 1864?
How can a soldier's experience shape how his family votes?
answers: Abraham Lincoln and George McClellan
His letters about the war could push his family toward the party that wanted to keep fighting, or toward the one that wanted peace
lessons.notes: Chunk the letters; one or two excerpts per child is plenty.

units.title: Unit 5: Prison Camps, Surrender, and the Meaning of Freedom

lessons.title: Andersonville: Prisoner of War Camp
steps: Look at the 1885 drawing and guess what the place was
Find Civil War prison camps and Andersonville on the maps
Read 'Life as a Prisoner' and study the 1864 photographs
Activity: research one prisoner's story

links.label: Lesson: Andersonville, Prisoner of War Camp (Teaching with Historic Places)

questions: In what state was Andersonville prison?
Why did both sides start holding prisoners for a long time?
answers: Georgia
The prisoner exchange system broke down in 1863

lessons.title: August Anguish at Andersonville: A Math Lesson
steps: Review mean, median, mode, and ratios
Use the August 1864 daily returns to work out the statistics on the worksheet
Write a short reflection: what do the numbers show about life in the prison?

links.label: Lesson plan: August Anguish at Andersonville (Andersonville NHS)
Daily returns, August 1864 (PDF)
Map of Andersonville Prison (PDF)

questions: About how many prisoners were held at Andersonville in summer 1864, and how many was it built for?
If 33,000 men were in a space built for 10,000, about how many times too crowded was it?
answers: About 33,000 in a space meant for 10,000
About 3.3 times

lessons.title: Perspectives After the Surrender at Appomattox
steps: Look at the picture of the McLean parlor and guess what happened there
Read the short biographies of Charles Wainwright, Fannie Berry, and Charles Minnigerode
Compare how each person felt about the end of the war

links.label: Lesson plan: Perspectives After the Surrender (Appomattox Court House NHP)
Worksheet 1: the McLean parlor (PDF)

questions: Who surrendered to whom in the McLean parlor on April 9, 1865?
What does 'perspective' mean?
answers: Robert E. Lee surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant
The different ways people can see the same event

lessons.title: Choosing a Path in Freedom
steps: List the jobs and skills it took to run Hampton, one of Maryland's largest plantations
Read about the choices formerly enslaved people at Hampton faced after Maryland ended slavery in 1864
Discuss how a person's skills could shape the path they chose in freedom

links.label: Lesson plan: Choosing a Path in Freedom (Hampton NHS)
Student activity book (Word)

questions: In what year did Maryland end slavery?
Why could freedom still be hard for newly freed people?
answers: They needed work, housing, and land, and faced discrimination

lessons.title: Frederick Douglass, Educator of Anacostia
steps: Read about Douglass's early life and why learning to read mattered so much to him
Read about the artifacts he collected and how he used them to teach
Use the lesson's activity sheets to 'read' a primary source like an archeologist

links.label: Lesson plan: Frederick Douglass, The Educator of Anacostia (Frederick Douglass NHS)
Activity sheet 1 (Word)

questions: Why did slaveholders fear enslaved people learning to read?
Who helped Douglass plan and pay for his escape?
What is archeology?
answers: Reading opened new ideas and communication, which threatened slavery
Anna Murray
The study of the human past through the things people left behind
